walkthroughs.body_html: District heating distributes hot water from a central source through insulated pipes to many buildings. Sources can include waste heat from power stations, biomass, geothermal or heat pumps. Copenhagen heats 98 percent of buildings this way. Compared with individual gas boilers it cuts emissions and improves efficiency by reusing waste heat.

Smart grids combine sensors, smart meters, two-way flows and demand response to integrate renewables. Households with rooftop solar can sell surplus to the grid. EV batteries can act as storage (vehicle-to-grid). Time-of-use tariffs shift demand to low-carbon hours, balancing variable wind and solar.

Circular cities design out waste. Materials are reused (deposit return for bottles), repaired (cafes), shared (libraries of things) and recycled. Food waste feeds anaerobic digesters producing biogas and digestate fertiliser. SUDS use swales and ponds to absorb rainwater. The aim is a city that mimics natural cycles, with minimal net resource input.
